paragraphs: Then she burst into tears again, but she held Mitya’s hand tight and would not let go.

“Mitya, darling, stay, don’t go. I have one thing to say to you,” she whispered, and suddenly lifted her face to him. “Listen, tell me who I love. I love one man here. Who is he? That’s what you have to tell me.”
A smile lit up her tear-swollen face, and her eyes shone in the half darkness.

“A falcon flew in, and my heart sank. ‘Fool! That’s the man you love!’ That’s what my heart whispered to me right away. You came in and everything grew bright. What’s he afraid of? I wondered. Because you were frightened; you couldn’t speak. He isn’t afraid of them—could you ever be frightened of anyone? It’s me he’s afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you little fool, how I called out to Alyosha from the window that I’d loved Mityenka for one hour, and that now I was going to love ... another. Mitya, Mitya, how could I be such a fool as to think I could love anyone after you? Do you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or not? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She jumped up and gripped his shoulders with both hands. Mitya, speechless with rapture, gazed into her eyes, at her face, at her smile, and suddenly he clasped her tightly in his arms and kissed her passionately.

“Will you forgive me for tormenting you? I tormented you all out of spite. It was out of spite that I drove the old man out of his mind.... Do you remember how you got drunk at my house one day and broke the wine glass? I remembered that, and today I broke a glass and drank ‘to my vile heart.’ Mitya, my falcon, why don’t you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he pulls back and looks and listens. Why listen to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, that’s right. If you love, then love! I’ll be your slave now, your slave for the rest of my life. It’s sweet to be a slave. Kiss me! Beat me, mistreat me, do what you like with me.... And I do deserve to suffer. Wait, stop, later, I won’t have that....” she suddenly pushed him away. “Go on, Mitya, I’ll come and have some wine, I want to be drunk, I’m going to get drunk and dance; I must, I must!” She tore herself away from him and disappeared behind the curtain. Mitya followed like a drunken man.

“Yes, come what may—whatever happens now, I’d give the whole world for one minute,” he thought. Grushenka did in fact toss off a whole glass of champagne in one gulp, and at once became very tipsy. She sat down in the same chair as before, with a blissful smile on her face. Her cheeks glowed, her lips burned, her flashing eyes were moist; there was a passionate appeal in them. Even Kalganov felt his heart stir, and he went up to her.

“Did you feel me kiss you just now, when you were asleep?” she said thickly. “I’m drunk now, that’s what it is.... And aren’t you drunk? And why isn’t Mitya drinking? Why don’t you drink, Mitya? I’m drunk, and you’re not drinking....”
“I am drunk! I’m drunk already ... drunk on you ... and now I’ll be drunk on wine, too.”

He drank another glass, and—he thought it strange himself—that glass made him completely drunk. He was suddenly drunk, although until that moment he had been perfectly sober; he remembered that. From then on everything whirled around him, as if he were delirious. He walked, laughed, talked to everybody, without knowing what he was doing. Only one persistent burning feeling kept making itself felt, “like a red-hot coal in his heart,” as he said afterwards. He went up to her, sat beside her, gazed at her, listened to her.... She became very talkative, kept calling everyone over, and beckoned to different girls from the chorus. When a girl came up, she either kissed her or made the sign of the cross over her. In another minute she might have cried. She was greatly amused by the “little old man,” as she called Maximov. He ran up every minute to kiss her hands, “each little finger,” and finally he danced another dance to an old song, which he sang himself. He danced with special vigor to the refrain:

The little pig says—umph! umph! umph! The little calf says—moo, moo, moo, The little duck says—quack, quack, quack, The little goose says—ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she’ll say!

“Give him something, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Give him a present, he’s poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted!... Do you know, Mitya, I’m going to go into a nunnery. No, I really will, one day. Alyosha said something to me today that I’ll remember all my life.... Yes.... But today let’s dance. Tomorrow the nunnery, but today we’ll dance. I want to play today, good people, and what of it? God will forgive us. If I were God, I’d forgive everyone: ‘My dear sinners, from this day forth I forgive you.’ I’m going to beg forgiveness myself: ‘Forgive me, good people, a silly wench.’ I’m a beast, that’s what I am. But I want to pray. I gave a little onion. Wicked as I’ve been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don’t stop them. Everyone in the world is good. Everyone—even the worst of them. The world’s a nice place. Bad as we are, the world’s all right. We’re good and bad, good and bad.... Come, tell me, I’ve something to ask you: come here, everyone, and I’ll ask you: Why am I so good? You know I am good. I’m very good.... Come, why am I so good?”

So Grushenka babbled on, getting more and more drunk. At last she announced that she was going to dance, too. She got up from her chair, staggering. “Mitya, don’t give me any more wine—if I ask you, don’t give it to me. Wine doesn’t give peace. Everything’s going round, the stove, and everything. I want to dance. Let everyone see how I dance ... let them see how beautifully I dance....”

She really meant it. She pulled a white cambric handkerchief out of her pocket and took it by one corner in her right hand, to wave in the dance. Mitya ran to and fro, the girls fell quiet and got ready to break into a dancing song at the first signal. Maximov, hearing that Grushenka wanted to dance, squealed with delight and ran skipping about in front of her, humming:
With legs so slim and sides so trim And its little tail curled tight.
But Grushenka flapped her handkerchief at him and shooed him off.

“Sh-h! Mitya, why don’t they come? Let everyone come ... to look on. Call them in too, the ones that were locked in.... Why did you lock them in? Tell them I’m going to dance. Let them look on, too....”
Mitya walked with a drunken swagger to the locked door and began knocking on it with his fist to call the Poles.
“Hey, you ... Podvysotskys! Come on, she’s going to dance. She’s calling you.”
“_Lajdak!_” one of the Poles shouted back.
“You’re a _lajdak_ yourself! You’re a little scoundrel, that’s what you are.”
“Stop making fun of Poland,” said Kalganov pompously. He was drunk too.
“Quiet, boy! If I call him a scoundrel, that doesn’t mean I’ve called all of Poland one. One _lajdak_ doesn’t make a Poland. Be quiet, my pretty boy, and eat a sweet.”

“Ach, what men! Behaving as if they weren’t men at all. Why won’t they make friends?” said Grushenka, and stepped forward to dance. The chorus broke into “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka threw back her head, half opened her lips, smiled, waved her handkerchief, and suddenly, with a violent lurch, stopped dead in the middle of the room, looking bewildered.
“I’m weak....” she said in an exhausted voice. “Forgive me.... I’m weak, I can’t.... I’m sorry.”
She bowed to the chorus, and then began bowing in all directions.
“I’m sorry.... Forgive me....”
“The lady’s been drinking. The pretty lady has been drinking,” voices were heard saying.
“The lady’s had too much to drink,” Maximov explained to the girls, giggling.
“Mitya, lead me away ... take me,” said Grushenka helplessly. Mitya pounced on her, swept her up in his arms, and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

“Well, I’ll be going now,” thought Kalganov. He walked out of the blue room and shut both halves of the door behind him. But the orgy in the larger room went on, louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

“Don’t touch me....” she faltered, in a pleading voice. “Don’t touch me until I’m yours.... I’ve told you I’m yours, but don’t touch me ... spare me.... With them here, so close, you mustn’t. He’s here. It’s nasty here....”
“I’ll obey you! I won’t even think of it ... I worship you!” muttered Mitya. “Yes, it’s nasty here, it’s vile.”
And still holding her in his arms, he sank to his knees beside the bed.

“I know that though you’re a brute, you’re generous,” Grushenka got out with difficulty. “It must be honorable ... from now on it will be honorable ... and let’s be honest, let’s be good, not brutes, but good ... take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don’t want it to be here, but far, far away....”
“Oh yes, yes, it must be!” said Mitya, pressing her in his arms. “I’ll take you and we’ll fly away.... Oh, I’d give my whole life, for one year only, to know about that blood!”
“What blood?” Grushenka asked, bewildered.
“Nothing,” Mitya muttered through his teeth. “Grusha, you wanted to be honest, but I’m a thief. I’ve stolen money from Katya.... Disgrace, what a disgrace!”

“From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn’t steal it. Give it back to her, take it from me.... Why make a fuss? Everything I have is yours now. What does money matter? We’ll waste it anyway.... People like us are bound to waste money. But we’d better go and work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We must work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won’t be your mistress, I’ll be faithful to you, I’ll be your slave, I’ll work for you. We’ll go to the young lady and bow down to her together, so that she’ll forgive us, and then we’ll go away. And if she won’t forgive us, we’ll go anyway. Take her the money and love me.... Don’t love her.... Don’t love her anymore. If you love her, I’ll strangle her.... I’ll put out both her eyes with a needle....”
“I love you. I love only you. I’ll love you in Siberia....”

“Why Siberia? Oh, all right, Siberia, if you like. I don’t care ... we’ll work ... there’s snow in Siberia.... I love driving in the snow ... and there have to be bells.... Do you hear, a bell’s ringing? Where is that bell ringing? Someone’s coming.... Now it’s stopped.”

She closed her eyes, exhausted, and fell asleep for a moment. There really had been the sound of a bell in the distance, but the ringing had stopped. Mitya let his head sink onto her breast. He did not notice that the bell had stopped ringing. Nor did he notice that the songs had stopped, and that instead of singing and drunken noise there was complete stillness in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

“What is it? Was I asleep? Yes ... a bell ... I fell asleep and dreamed I was driving over the snow with bells, and I dozed. I was with someone I loved, with you. And far, far away. I was holding you and kissing you, nestling close to you. I was cold, and the snow glistened.... You know how the snow glistens at night when the moon shines. It was as if I wasn’t on earth. I woke up, and my dear one is right beside me. How sweet that is!...”

“Right beside you,” murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her bosom, her hands. And suddenly a strange idea came to him: it seemed that she was looking straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but over his head, with an intent, almost uncanny stare. A look of wonder, almost of alarm, came suddenly over her face.
“Mitya, who’s that looking at us?” she whispered.
Mitya turned and saw that someone had indeed parted the curtains and seemed to be watching them. And it seemed to be more than one person.
He jumped up and quickly went toward the intruder.
“Come here, come over to us,” said a voice, not loud, but firm and commanding.

Mitya stepped through to the other side of the curtain and stood stock still. The room was full of people, but not the ones who had been there before. A shiver ran down his back at once, and he shuddered. He recognized every one of those people instantly. That tall, stout old man in the overcoat and the forage cap with a cockade was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And that “consumptive-looking” trim dandy, “who always has such polished boots”—that was the deputy prosecutor. “He has a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me.” And that small young man in spectacles.... Mitya forgot his surname, though he knew him and had seen him: he was the “investigating lawyer,” from the “school of jurisprudence,” who had only lately come to the town. And this man—the inspector of police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a man he knew well. And those fellows with the brass plates on, why were they here? And those other two ... peasants.... And there at the door Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch....
“Gentlemen! What is this, gentlemen?” Mitya began, but suddenly, as if beside himself, not knowing what he was doing, he cried out at the top of his voice:
“I un—der—stand!”
The young man in spectacles suddenly moved forward, stepped up to Mitya, and began, with dignity but in a hurry:
“We have to make ... in short, I must ask you to come this way, over here to the sofa.... It is absolutely imperative that you give an explanation.”
“The old man!” Mitya cried frantically. “The old man and his blood!... I understand.”
And he sank, almost fell, onto a chair close by, as if he had been cut down by a scythe.
“You understand? He understands it! Monster and parricide! Your father’s blood cries out against you!” the old police captain suddenly roared, stepping up to Mitya.
He was beside himself, crimson in the face and trembling all over.
“This is impossible!” cried the small young man. “Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won’t do!... Please let me speak. I never would have expected such behavior from you....”

“This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium,” cried the police captain. “Look at him: drunk, at this time of night, in the company of a disreputable woman, with his father’s blood on his hands.... It’s delirium!...”
“I urge you most earnestly, dear Mihail Makarovitch, to hold back your feelings,” the prosecutor said in a rapid whisper to the old police captain, “or I will be forced to resort to—”
But the little lawyer did not let him finish. He turned to Mitya and spoke in a loud, firm, dignified voice:
“Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, it is my duty to inform you that you are charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed tonight....”
He said something more, and the prosecutor added something too, but although Mitya heard them, he did not understand. He stared at them all with wild eyes.
